Where it began

Joel Garner was born on 16 December 1952 in Enterprise, a small village among the cane fields of Christ Church, Barbados. He was the elder of two boys and played cricket from an early age, and at Foundation Boys school he batted as well as bowled.

The turning point came when Seymour Nurse, coaching a school side, took one look at the tall young man and told him someone his size belonged at the bowling crease, running in fast. Charlie Griffith later added a swinging yorker and a well-aimed bouncer.

The player

Garner took over from Sobers as Littleborough's professional in the Central Lancashire League in 1976, and in three seasons there he took 334 wickets at 9.34. Somerset signed him for 1977. He took 338 first-class wickets for them at 18.10 and shared in the five trophies of the county's most successful years. Two of his finest days came in Lord's finals: six for 29 in the 1979 Gillette Cup and five for 14 in the 1981 Benson & Hedges Cup.

His Test career began against Pakistan in 1977, with 25 wickets in his first series. In 58 Tests up to 1987 he took 259 wickets at 20.98, with seven five-wicket hauls and a best of six for 56. He also captained Barbados in 1986, and was part of a West Indies side that went 15 years without losing a Test series.

What made him special

At 6ft 8in he was, in his day, the tallest fast bowler Test cricket had seen, and he made the ball rear up from a good length. Batsmen could not drive him, and if they stayed back the yorker was waiting. In one-day cricket he was even tougher to score off, with 146 wickets in 98 matches at just 3.09 runs an over. In the 1979 World Cup final against England he took five for 39, with a burst of five for 4, and twice stood on a hat-trick.

Batting was a gentler pastime. He scored 672 Test runs at 12.44, with a solitary fifty. Even so, at the 1983 World Cup he and Andy Roberts put on 71 for the last wicket against India, then a World Cup record.

Away from the middle

Garner was named a Wisden Cricketer of the Year, and in 2010 the ICC welcomed him into its Hall of Fame. That same year he managed the West Indies on their tour of Sri Lanka. He has also served as a West Indies selector and led the West Indies effort in Masters cricket, and by 2016 he was president of the Barbados Cricket Association.

And finally

He once explained his side's plan to Derek Pringle. He and Malcolm Marshall would take the new ball and remove the top order, the others would keep things tight, and then the two of them would return to finish off the tail. After a spell with the bat, they would do it all over again. Geoff Boycott had his own answer to the problem: he joked that someone ought to shorten Garner at the knees so he would bowl from a normal height.
